description: Regional energy grid infrastructure, high-voltage utility demand, and public safety concerns common to both data centers and battery energy storage systems; staff reported needing the full extended year to finish the data center ordinance after spending the prior year on the energy-storage-system framework. Active (extended) as of 2026-09-23. The County Board voted unanimously on August 18, 2026 to extend the moratorium on data centers (originally adopted August 2025) for a second consecutive year, through August 19, 2027, finding that allowing it to lapse would threaten public safety and orderly development because current regulations are inadequate. Planning and Zoning Administrator Trevor Bordelon said his office would need the full additional year to develop the data-center ordinance, having spent the prior year on a parallel energy-storage-system framework intended to serve as a foundation for high-load utility planning generally. Legal basis: Temporary interim zoning ordinance on data centers, adopted by the Freeborn County Board of Commissioners in August 2025 (alongside a parallel moratorium on energy storage systems, due to overlapping grid-infrastructure concerns); extended for a second year (through Aug. 19, 2027) by unanimous County Board resolution on August 18, 2026, under Minnesota Statutes Chapter 394.

description: Commissioners cited possible effects on water, power, noise, drainage, and public health from large new solar, wind, battery-storage, and data-center developments outside city limits, describing the pause as 'due diligence'; no specific project was pending at the time of adoption. Active as of 2026-09-23; set to expire 2027-09-08 absent a single permitted extension of up to six additional months. Residents and at least one local business owner (who called the measure 'backdoor zoning') have publicly questioned whether the county had legal authority to adopt it without voter-approved planning and zoning; commissioners have declined to comment publicly and the county's own attorney has not returned press inquiries. Legal basis: Cedar County ordinance imposing a 12-month moratorium, adopted by commissioners 2026-09-08, citing (among other authority) RSMo §49.650 and county public-health authority; legal commentators note §49.650 by its terms applies to first-, second-, and fourth-class noncharter counties while Cedar County is third class, raising an open legal question about the ordinance's validity.

description: Pause on accepting, processing, or issuing permits, licenses, and applications for new data centers and battery energy storage systems while the city develops zoning and regulatory standards. Active as of 2026-09-23 (the 180-day moratorium is set to run through 2027-01-02 absent extension). Permanent data-center/BESS zoning rules remain in process: the City Council discussed proposed new standards but pushed its final vote back at least a month after confusion among residents and councilmembers, with City Manager Troy Anderson confirming the moratorium itself is unaffected by that separate vote; Mayor Kevin King said he would look into organizing a public hearing before the council revisits the permanent rules in October 2026. Similar temporary pauses remain in effect in unincorporated Jackson County and neighboring Leavenworth County, Kansas. Legal basis: Resolution No. 7238 (City Council agenda item 26-741), 'A resolution declaring a 180-day moratorium on the processing of applications related to and issuance of city permits or licenses related to the installation or use of data processing and hosting facilities located in the City of Independence, Missouri, for projects or applications not already submitted to, authorized, or approved by the City,' sponsored by Councilmember Stewart and passed 7-0 on 2026-07-06. A companion Resolution No. 7239 (agenda item 26-742) imposed a parallel 180-day moratorium on battery energy storage system (BESS) facilities, also passed 7-0 the same night.

description: Rapid emergence of data center and battery energy storage system applications; perceived gaps in the Jackson County Unified Development Code; infrastructure, environmental, public safety, and public notice concerns. Adopted by the County Legislature (8 in favor, 1 excused) on 2026-06-22 as a 180-day moratorium on data-center and BESS land-use applications, for the purpose of developing long-term policy, County Code provisions, and enhanced public-notice requirements. Whether the measure was signed by County Executive Phil LeVota, became law without signature, or was vetoed was not independently confirmed in this pass; no veto was reported in any subsequent coverage found. Legal basis: Ordinance 6074, introduced 2026-04-06 by Legislator Sean E. Smith (120-day version); a competing 365-day version (Ordinance 6087, sponsored by Legislative Chair Manny Abarca) was also considered in committee as of 2026-06-01. The full County Legislature passed a 180-day moratorium on data-center and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) land-use applications by an 8-1 vote (one member excused) on 2026-06-22. description: Butler County has no zoning; a countywide survey (~800 responses) found roughly 90% support for a moratorium on the top land uses of concern (wind, solar, data centers, battery storage, landfill), following years of unregulated development including the in-progress Sandhills Energy solar project. Active as of 2026-09-23, though modified: adopted 2026-03-16 as a 9-month moratorium (through approximately 2026-12-15) on wind, solar, data center, battery storage, and landfill land uses while the county completes a comprehensive plan and zoning regulations (targeted for completion around September 2026). Per Flatwater Free Press, after the threat of a lawsuit the county later exempted the ongoing Sandhills Energy solar project (which had been under development since 2019) from the moratorium. Legal basis: Resolution 2026-07 (Butler County Board of Supervisors), mirroring the Planning Commission's Resolution 2026-04 but striking language that would have excluded projects already under construction.

The board separately voted to seek a legal review of 2025-2026 zoning-ordinance amendments that eased approval conditions for the proposed data center, including whether a conflict of interest by a then-board-chair voids those amendments, and whether the pending conditional use permit applications for the data center and battery storage facility remain legally eligible for consideration pending that review. Legal basis: Not yet enacted. On 2026-09-22 the Township Board unanimously passed a motion (moved by Board Chair Dustin Burchill) to hold a formal public hearing on whether to adopt a two-year moratorium; the specific ordinance language has not been finalized.

description: Comprehensive health and safety review of AI data centers and battery energy storage systems. Active as of 2026-09-23. The Commissioners Court unanimously adopted the signed order on 2026-07-27 following the July 13, 2026 public hearing; KWHI (2026-07-28) independently confirms the unanimous vote and describes the order's scope (equipment-manufacturer audits, an Energy Development Zone siting study by the County Fire Marshal and County Engineer, and injunctive-relief enforcement authority). No repeal, rescission, or completion of the review was found in sources reviewed through 2026-09-23. KWHI notes Austin County is 'the second county in Texas to adopt a moratorium of this nature,' after Hill County (which later rescinded its moratorium following a developer lawsuit; see the existing tx-hill-county-2026 row). Legal basis: Order of Austin County, Texas, Regarding Battery Energy Storage Systems and Data Centers Health and Safety Review, adopted by the Commissioners Court on 2026-07-27 under Texas Health and Safety Code section 121.003 and Texas Local Government Code section 352.016, among other authorities. The signed, executed order was located directly on austincounty.com (distinct from the earlier unsigned draft). It suspends county permit, plan-review, and inspection approvals for BESS and data center construction in unincorporated areas until a 'Comprehensive Health and Safety Review' (covering fire/life-safety, cybersecurity/foreign-adversary equipment verification tied to the Lone Star Infrastructure Protection Act and the Governor's Prohibited Technologies List, and an Energy Development Zone siting study) is complete, with the Commissioners Court retaining sole discretion over when that review is finished. It requires County Fire Marshal plan review/approval and an independent third-party engineering evaluation before construction, and authorizes the County's legal counsel to seek injunctive relief against violators.

description: Linn County replaced its utility-scale solar moratorium with siting rules in its Unified Development Code: solar equipment 300 ft from dwellings unless the owner waives it, 120 ft from perennial streams and ditches, 50 ft from property lines in the Renewable Energy overlay district; battery storage 200 ft from property lines and rights-of-way and 500 ft from off-site occupied structures unless waived; 55 dBA day and 50 dBA night noise limits; RE overlay rezoning and a passing score on the county's solar scorecard. Concentrating solar power is prohibited, and fenced arrays over 160 acres need a wildlife corridor.
long_description: setback: solar panels, structures and electrical equipment (excluding fences and interconnection lines) 300 ft from dwellings unless the owner waives it in writing (recorded); 120 ft from the centerline of perennial stream corridors and open ditches; 50 ft from property lines in the Renewable Energy overlay district (may be reduced to zero next to another overlay use). Battery energy storage: 200 ft from a property line or right-of-way; 500 ft from the nearest property line including an occupied structure off the subject property, reducible to 200 ft by a recorded, notarized waiver from that owner; 120 ft from perennial stream corridors and open ditches; sited inside a new solar facility when built with one. overlay_zone: rezoning to the Renewable Energy overlay district and the minimum passing threshold on the Linn County Utility Scale Solar Scorecard. noise_limit: hourly average 55 dBA by day (sunrise to sunset) and 50 dBA at night (sunset to sunrise) at the occupied dwelling of an adjacent residential property, or ambient Leq plus 5 dBA where ambient is higher; neighbours may waive in writing. Other: concentrating solar power (CSP) systems prohibited; fenced array areas over 160 acres require a wildlife corridor; panels at least 24 in. above ground at maximum tilt.

notes: Replaces the 2022 to 2023 utility-scale solar moratorium (Sabin REC-0118, held back as lifted; last set to expire Sept. 30, 2023). This copy leaves the ordinance number and the Gazette publication date blank. It records Planning and Zoning Commission Aug. 16, 2023; public hearing and first consideration Sept. 5, 2023; second consideration Sept. 13, 2023; third consideration and final passage Sept. 20, 2023. Also opened: The Gazette, https://www.thegazette.com/local-government/government-notes-linn-county-supervisors-pass-solar-ordinance/ : the Board of Supervisors 'unanimously adopted tighter restrictions for utility-scale solar installations', approved the score card 2-1 (Running-Marquardt and Rogers for, Zumbach against), and 'The changes won't apply to previously approved projects'. description: Cherokee County, Kansas adopted Resolution R-27-2025 on Dec. 22, 2025: a nine-month moratorium on approving requests to use county roads, resources or infrastructure for commercial renewable energy projects (wind turbines or solar panels generating power for sale), cryptocurrency mining, data centers, battery energy storage systems, new or unpermitted landfills and transfer stations, quarries and nuclear energy plants, and a ban on constructing any of these in the unincorporated county during the term. Resolution 11-2026, adopted June 8, 2026, re-adopted the same moratorium through March 31, 2027, while the county weighs a comprehensive plan and zoning.
long_description: moratorium: no approval of requests to use county roads, resources or infrastructure for, and no construction of, any commercial renewable energy project (multiple wind turbines and/or solar panels generating power for sale and off-site use, including roads, turbine foundations, panels and lines), cryptocurrency mining operation, data center, battery energy storage system, new or unpermitted landfill or transfer station, quarry or nuclear plant in the unincorporated county. R-27-2025: nine months from Dec. 22, 2025. Resolution 11-2026: effective June 8, 2026, expires March 31, 2027. Fine up to $1,000 per day.

description: In October 2023, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors cast a 3-2 vote to establish a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for the development of renewable energy on private property.
long_description: In October 2023, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors cast a 3-2 vote to establish a 240-day moratorium on using energy overlay re-zoning for the development of renewable energy on private property. In the four months prior to the moratorium’s adoption, the Board of Supervisors had denied every application for energy overlay re-zoning, including those for which the county’s planning and zoning commission recommended approval. Prior to the moratorium’s adoption, a local attorney opined that it would violate Arizona Statute 11-833, which limits moratoria on rural land to situations in which a county has demonstrated that a moratorium is necessary to “prevent irrevocable public harm” from a “clear and imminent danger.” In June 2024, the Mohave County Board of Supervisors voted 3-2 in favor of allowing solar projects within the county on land zoned for “Light Industrial” use, effectively lifting the prior moratorium.

description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice.
long_description: In May 2023, the San Miguel County Board of Commissioners enacted a 6-month moratorium on applications for commercial energy projects (including solar projects), which was scheduled to expire in November 2024 after being extended twice. In September 2024, the Board unanimously adopted new zoning regulations on solar projects, ending the moratorium. The zoning regulations prioritize the siting of solar projects in areas that are already impacted by development. Large-scale solar projects of 30 acres or more are only permitted in certain districts and are not permitted in the Wright’s Mesa Light Industrial and Wright’s Mesa Rural Agricultural districts. Structures on solar farms are also required to be set back at least 200 feet from property lines.

description: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance.
long_description: On September 24, 2024, Clinton County’s Planning and Zoning Commission issued a three-month moratorium on commercial wind farm applications as they revised the county’s 2008 wind ordinance. This moratorium was extended in December 2024 and will run through June 2025. A community opposition group, Clinton & Jackson County Iowa Residents Against Wind Turbines, has collected over 700 signatures for a petition against the project and has been active in public hearings regarding the proposed ordinance. [Note: As of January 2025, the proposed ordinance from the County Commission leaves little land available for commercial wind. The required setbacks for wind would be 5 miles in either direction from byway roads, 1,500 feet from property lines, and two miles from any incorporated city. A proposed wind project from NextEra Energy, which would have a capacity of 250 MW, would most likely be held back if the county supervisors approved the commission’s updated ordinance.]

description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance.
long_description: In 2017, Ford County imposed a moratorium on wind energy projects while it revised its ordinance. In 2018, the county board’s zoning committee recommended increasing the existing 1,000-foot setback from buildings to 2,250 feet. At a hearing in October 2018, a group called Ford County Citizens for Property Rights demanded 3,250-foot setbacks from any property lines. On September 13, 2021, the County Board adopted an amended wind ordinance that increased setback to 2,250 feet from property lines upon which a primary structure is located. The ordinance further specified that, even if neighbors agreed to waive the setback requirement, any wind tower still must be at least 1,000 feet from the nearest primary structure. description: As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built.
severity_basis: ban or moratorium (the source does not say which)
long_description: As of April 2019, twelve of the fifteen towns within Henry County had passed resolutions establishing buffer zones where no wind projects could be built. These buffers extend approximately 4 miles around each town. The twelve towns included Cadiz, Sulphur Springs, Kennard, Blountsville, Greensboro, Lewisville, Mount Summit, Springport, Straughn, and Middletown. In May 2019, Indiana passed a law limiting municipalities’ authority to enact such buffer zones going forward and voiding any such ordinances or resolution adopted after December 31, 2018. The law did not void any ordinances or resolutions adopted before January 1, 2019. Eleven of the Henry County town resolutions were grandfathered in under the law, but the town of Middletown’s was not.

description: In response to NextEra Energy’s proposal to construct a wind farm, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development in December 2013, which lasted until April 2014.
long_description: In response to NextEra Energy’s proposal to construct a wind farm, the Douglas County Commission issued a moratorium on wind farm development in December 2013, which lasted until April 2014. In 2022, Douglas County adopted a solar ordinance that limits cumulative solar farm acreage in the county to 1,000 acres and requires solar panels and arrays to be at least 500 feet from any existing residence. In May 2024, after a public hearing, the Commission voted to adopt new wind regulations that increased setbacks from property lines to 2,500 feet. About two-thirds of commenters at the public hearing expressed opposition to wind energy projects in the county, with some requesting a wind energy ban. Others argued that the regulations were excessive and that the setbacks would effectively prevent wind energy development. One frequent commenter was arrested on suspicion of interfering with the conduct of public business

description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county.
long_description: In December 2021, the Reno County Commission banned wind development in all zoned areas of the county. The vote to ban wind development in certain areas of the county came three years after residents requested that the commission impose a moratorium on wind development, ostensibly in response to news that NextEra was purchasing leases for a potential wind farm in the county. As of December 2021, a moratorium on commercial wind development was scheduled to run through March 2022. As of February 2023, the county’s zoning regulations provide that, “[i]n order to provide for an incorporated city to extend its corporate boundary and increase its tax base, no turbine shall be located within 1 mile of an incorporated city boundary.” Wind farms are permitted, however, in a designated Commercial Wind Energy Conversion Systems District in the unincorporated part of the county.

description: In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations.
long_description: In September 2023, Sedgwick Country enacted a 6-month moratorium on solar applications as it considered new solar regulations. In March 2024, the Sedgwick County Commission extended the September 2023 moratorium on new commercial solar farms until September 2024. In August 2024, the county adopted new regulations, officially ending the moratorium. The new regulations prohibit solar projects from exceeding 1,500 acres in area; prohibit solar projects from being located in or on more than 6 contiguous sections of land; and require new solar projects be set back at least 2 miles from the nearest solar project.

description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County.
long_description: The Woodson County Board of County Commissioners has enacted a moratorium and prohibition on Commercial Renewable Energy Projects in the unincorporated area of Woodson County. Specifically, the resolution directs the suspension of acting on any application for a Conditional Use Permit or permits for the erection and construction of any Commercial Renewable Energy Project (Section 1), prohibits the establishment of any such project (Section 3), and declares such establishment a violation of public interest while the resolution is in effect. No applications for Conditional Use permits shall be set for public hearing prior to 12 months from adoption (Section 2). The moratorium may be extended, terminated earlier, or amended by subsequent resolution (Section 5). The resolution “shall remain in effect until the end of February 2026” (Section 6). There are no stated conditions or exceptions limiting the prohibition to specific areas, prior approvals, or compliance status. The moratorium is currently in effect as of December 5, 2025.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones.
long_description: The City of Waltham’s zoning code effectively limited large-scale solar energy facilities to industrial zones. A developer who owned land in Waltham and a neighboring town sought permission from the city building inspector to build an access road on the land the developer owned in Waltham to a proposed 1-MW solar facility in a neighboring town. The building inspector denied permission on the basis of local zoning restrictions. On June 4, 2022, the Supreme Judicial Court struck down the restrictions, finding that “[a]n outright ban of large-scale solar energy systems in all but one to two percent of a municipality’s land area . . . restricts rather than promotes the legislative goal of promoting solar energy” and that, “in the absence of a reasonable basis grounded in public health, safety, or welfare, such a prohibition is impermissible.”  Note that this is included as a pre-March 2022 development because the relevant restriction was in place before March 2022.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws.
long_description: In May 2023, Pelham residents voted to amend the town’s solar and energy storage bylaws. The town prohibited energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and required all large-scale solar projects (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to be set back at least 500 feet from nearby streets. The town further required developers to set aside 4 times the total area of a solar installation for forestland conservation, if the project would convert any existing forestland for solar development. In December 2023, the Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to the town rejecting portions of the amended bylaw, including the forestland conservation requirement, noting that certain bylaw provisions failed to comply with state law that prohibits municipalities from banning solar installations through zoning.

description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions.
long_description: Shutesbury’s solar bylaw, adopted in May 2008 and amended in June 2021, prohibits solar plants larger than fifteen acres, among other restrictions. In January 2023, Shutesbury residents voted to adopt a revised town bylaw for solar arrays at a Special Town Meeting. The revised bylaw would have banned energy storage systems as a principal use in all zoning districts and limited large-scale solar installations (defined as installations between 1.5 and 15 acres of land) to a special use in Forest Conservation Districts, prohibiting such installations in all other districts. The Massachusetts Attorney General’s office sent a letter to Shutesbury officials disapproving of the January 2023 bylaw, partially based on a determination that the bylaw violated state law by effectively banning solar installations. The Attorney General’s office’s action resulted in the pre-2023 bylaw regaining legal effect. The pre-2023 bylaw is the subject of a lawsuit filed by developer PureSky Energy in August 2023, in which PureSky alleges that the town’s solar regulations are in violation of state law that prohibits unreasonable regulation of solar energy systems.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: On March 9, 2023, Carroll County adopted a 6-month moratorium on applications for community solar farms on land currently zoned for agricultural purposes.
mechanisms: cap on project size (solar), visual_impact_rule (solar), setback (solar)
long_description: On March 9, 2023, Carroll County adopted a 6-month moratorium on applications for community solar farms on land currently zoned for agricultural purposes. In December 2024, the Carroll County Board of Commissioners amended its land use ordinance to increase restrictions on commercial solar projects. Under the new ordinance, ground-mounted solar systems in residential and commercial districts cannot exceed 480 square feet, and projects must be set back at least 400 feet from any public transportation corridors. In addition, the height of ground-mounted systems cannot exceed 15 feet, and facilities must include a 12-foot-tall vegetative buffer along all property lines.

description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource.
long_description: In November 2015, the Town of Freedom enacted a wind turbine ordinance that requires all wind turbines be set back 2,500 feet from any Scenic or Special Resource. Depending on the height and megawatt capacity of the turbine, the ordinance requires it be setback either 1.5 times turbine height, 3 times turbine height, or 13 times turbine height from non-participating landowners. Turbines less than 100 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 1.5 times turbine height; turbines between 100 and 150 feet in height and less than or equal to 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 3 times turbine height; and turbines greater than 150 feet in height and/or greater than 10 kW in capacity must be set back at least 13 times turbine height. The ordinance measures turbine height by the highest point of any turbine blade tip. Shadow flicker is limited to ten hours per year, and depending on the time of day and height of turbine, noise is limited to between 30 and 40 dBa.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In April 2016, the Ellington Township Board of Trustees held a special meeting to vote on whether to enact a wind energy moratorium.
long_description: In April 2016, the Ellington Township Board of Trustees held a special meeting to vote on whether to enact a wind energy moratorium. By a unanimous vote, the board agreed to a 4-month moratorium on wind turbine development. The moratorium was supported by a group called Ellington-Almer Township Concerned Citizens, and it resulted in the delay of the Tuscola III wind farm.  The Ellington Township Zoning Ordinance, as amended July 2021, requires that wind turbines be set back by a distance of 5 times turbine height from property lines of non-participating parcels (i.e., 2,500 feet for a 500-foot turbine), and 3 times turbine height from any road. The ordinance further provides that noise shall not exceed 40 dBA at any time on a nonparticipating property and prohibits any shadow flicker on neighboring properties.

long_description: In March 2020, the Matteson Township Board voted to adopt restrictions on wind energy, including by limiting turbine height to 328 feet as measured from the blade tip, despite objections from the developer of a proposed wind project that 500 feet is the typical height of commercial wind turbines in the area. The ordinance also requires a setback of 1.25 miles from property lines, which effectively excludes wind energy projects from more than 50% of the township, and requires zero shadow flicker on neighboring properties. As with Batavia Township and Sherwood Township, the restrictions were promoted aggressively on Facebook by a group called Concerned Citizens of Branch County in response to efforts by DTE Energy to develop a wind farm in the area, which was ultimately put on hold in August 2020.

description: On October 23, 2024, Wibaux County became the first county in Montana to adopt countywide zoning to restrict wind development.
long_description: On October 23, 2024, Wibaux County became the first county in Montana to adopt countywide zoning to restrict wind development. The new zoning rules require wind turbines to be set back 1,250 from property lines and 1.5 miles from residences. The rules were adopted as part of an effort to block AES’s proposal to construct the 235-MW Wibaux Wind Farm, which would include 50 MW of battery storage.

description: In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted 5-1 to change setback rules for wind turbines from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings.
long_description: In May 2024, the Knox County Board of Supervisors voted 5-1 to change setback rules for wind turbines from 2,000 feet to 6,600 feet from nonparticipating dwellings. A wind energy company, which had been working to develop a 600-MW project in the county, filed a lawsuit against the county alleging that the zoning rule changes were made “with the express purpose of regulating” the wind energy company and its proposed wind project. On May 7, 2025, the Planning Commission voted to recommend a ban on commercial wind and solar development in the county. On June 11, 2025, the County Board of Supervisors voted to adopt the Planning Commission’s recommendation to ban any new commercial wind or solar projects. See entry on North Fork Wind (Knox County) for more information.

long_description: The Saline County Zoning Regulations, as amended in 2018, require that wind turbines be set back 0.5 miles from occupied structures on abutting properties. After the 6-1 vote, the Board stated that the moratorium was meant to ensure community safety and the sustainable future development of wind energy in Saline County.

description: In September 2021, the Town of Vestal enacted a 6-month moratorium on approval of solar farms 25 kW or larger.
long_description: In September 2021, the Town of Vestal enacted a 6-month moratorium on approval of solar farms 25 kW or larger. In May 2022, the moratorium was extended by 1 year, and in May 2023, it was extended by another 6 months.  In June 2024, the Vestal Town Board unanimously voted to instate a 1-year moratorium on the approval of commercial solar farms, halting existing and future applications for solar farms. At public hearings on the moratorium, some residents expressed concerns about the potential negative impacts of solar farms, such as fire hazards and water contamination. In June 2025, the town adopted Local Law 4 to regulate Solar Energy Systems, effectively ending the moratorium. The law provides that commercial solar development is only allowed in the Commercial Development, Industrial, and Industrial Development Districts.

long_description: In March 2024, the Town of Hoosick passed a 1-year moratorium on the permitting and siting of commercial solar farms with capacity greater than 5 MW. In May 2024, the town adopted a 1-year moratorium on the permitting and siting of wind energy conversion systems. The solar and wind moratoriums allowed the possibility of two 180-day extensions. In December 2024, the town adopted an amendment to its Energy Systems Law to regulate wind and solar development, effectively ending the moratorium. The law provides that Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems (greater than 5 MW) are only allowed in the Light Industrial/Commercial district.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In February 2024, the Town of Johnstown imposed a 6-month moratorium on solar and battery storage systems.
long_description: In February 2024, the Town of Johnstown imposed a 6-month moratorium on solar and battery storage systems. The moratorium was renewed in September 2024. In February 2025, the town extended the moratorium for an additional 6 months. In October 2025, the town adopted Local Law 3 to regulate solar energy facilities, effectively ending the moratorium on solar development. The law provides that Tier 4 Solar Energy Systems (up to 25 MW) are only allowed in the AUZ, RA, and M-1 Zones and that Tier 5 Solar Energy Systems (greater than 25 MW) are prohibited in the town. As to battery energy storage systems, the town extended the moratorium for an additional 6 months, through 2026.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: In November 2023, Mahoning County commissioners unanimously approved Green Township’s ban on large wind and solar projects in unincorporated parts of the township pursuant to S.B. 52.
jurisdiction: Green, Austintown, Beaver, Berlin, Canfield, Coitsville, Goshen, Jackson, Milton, Poland, and Springfield Townships
long_description: In November 2023, Mahoning County commissioners unanimously approved Green Township’s ban on large wind and solar projects in unincorporated parts of the township pursuant to S.B. 52. A public hearing was held in Green Township at the end of October 2023, in which residents were largely supportive of banning wind and solar. The ban had the effect of blocking the planned 150-MW Alpin Sun solar project. In February 2024, the Mahoning County Commission approved extending the ban to 10 additional townships within the county, namely: Austintown, Beaver, Berlin, Canfield, Coitsville, Goshen, Jackson, Milton, Poland, and Springfield.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: On July 17, 2025, the Richland Board of County Commissioners adopted a resolution to ban on utility-scale wind and solar development in 11 of the county’s 18 townships.
long_description: On July 17, 2025, the Richland Board of County Commissioners adopted a resolution to ban on utility-scale wind and solar development in 11 of the county’s 18 townships. Local residents formed a group called Richland County Citizens for Property Rights and Job Development, which is working to get the ban reversed. The group circulated a petition calling for a referendum on the Commissioners’ resolution. The petition garnered 3,380 signatures, enough for the issue to be put on to voters at the next primary elections in May 2026.

long_description: In March 2024, the Kiskiminetas Township Planning Commission began discussions to revise the Township’s Commercial Solar Energy Systems (CSES) Ordinance. The new ordinance imposes a $50,000 annual development fee per 1-MW of nameplate capacity for large-scale solar projects, as well as a non-refundable $2,500 application fee. description: In July 2024, the Smith Township Planning Commission began discussions to amend its solar and battery energy storage ordinance.
severity_basis: ban or moratorium (the source does not say which)
long_description: In July 2024, the Smith Township Planning Commission began discussions to amend its solar and battery energy storage ordinance. On November 12, 2024, with the unanimous recommendation of the Planning Commission, the Board of Supervisors unanimously adopted the new ordinance 2024-5. The amendments include: increasing the setbacks from any occupied structures from 300 feet to 500 feet; adding Principal Solar Energy Systems (PSES) and Battery Energy Storage Systems (BESS) to the Conservation District (C-D) as a conditional use and removing those from the Rural Residential (A-1) District; requiring an endangered species report; requiring a decommissioning plan to be submitted during land development and updated every three years instead of every five years; requiring a decommissioning bond to be set at 125% and reviewed every three years; and requiring a review from the Historical Society.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

long_description: In January 2011, the Town of North Kingstown placed a 6-month moratorium, which was extended by 90 days in June 2011. In November 2011, the Town Council voted to prohibit all wind turbines in the town pending the issuance of a state report anticipated in early 2012. The moratorium was motivated by opposition to a proposal to construct two wind turbines in the town. However, those two turbines were not subject to the moratorium. As of March 2023, wind energy systems are prohibited in the town, not including any approved prior to November 21, 2011.

description: In May 2017, the Hughes County Commission approved a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development in order to review setback requirements in the local zoning ordinance.
long_description: In May 2017, the Hughes County Commission approved a 6-month moratorium on wind energy development in order to review setback requirements in the local zoning ordinance. One commissioner expressed concerns about competing land uses between wind and cattle grazing, while noting that he did not want to restrict economic development. In August 2020, the Hughes County Commission amended its zoning ordinance to require a setback of 2,640 feet (0.5 miles) or 4.9 times the height of the tower. The setback may be reduced to 1,400 feet with a waiver from the landowner.

description: Letcher Township increased setbacks to 1 mile from dwellings of non-participating homeowners and 1,500 feet from property lines.
long_description: In 2016, residents of Letcher Township in Sanborn County pre-emptively mobilized to block Juhl Energy from developing a wind project. Although Juhl Energy had not yet submitted an application, residents were concerned that the company would look to Letcher Township after nearby Davison County rejected its applicaion for a 9-to-11-turbine wind farm. Out of 77 registered voters in Letcher Township, 50 signed a petition opposing the project. In response to the petition, the Board of Supervisors voted to increase setbacks to 1 mile from dwellings of non-participating homeowners and 1,500 feet from property lines, making the project impossible to site.

description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA)—one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions—unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems.
jurisdiction: Caledonia County; Essex County; Orleans County
severity_basis: ban or moratorium (the source does not say which)
long_description: In January 2015, the Northeastern Vermont Development Association (NVDA)—one of eleven Vermont regional planning commissions—unanimously approved a resolution against the development of all industrial wind energy systems. The resolution states that “[i]t is the position of the NVDA that no further development of industrial-scale wind turbines should take place in the Northeast Kingdom.” This position was reaffirmed in NVDA’s 2018 Energy Plan and in NVDA’s June 2023 memorandum readopting that plan. NVDA’s resolution is not legally binding and is intended to serve as a “starting point” for member municipalities’ zoning process. These member municipalities are Caledonia, Essex, and Orleans counties.
source: Sabin Center, Opposition to Renewable Energy Facilities in the United States (Sept. 2026 ed.), via data/renewable_opposition_records_2026-09.csv

description: Huron County commissioners adopted Resolution 26-110 on April 7, 2026, designating all of the unincorporated area of the county's 19 townships as restricted areas where large wind farms and large solar facilities are prohibited under Ohio Rev. Code 303.58. Economically significant wind farms are also prohibited in 17 of the townships but not in Ripley and Wakeman Townships.
long_description: Large wind farms and large solar facilities (as defined in ORC 4906.01) prohibited in all unincorporated territory of all 19 townships. Economically significant wind farms (as defined in ORC 4906.13) also prohibited in Bronson, Clarksfield, Fairfield, Fitchville, Greenfield, Greenwich, Hartland, Lyme, New Haven, New London, Norwalk, Norwich, Peru, Richmond, Ridgefield, Sherman and Townsend Townships. Ripley and Wakeman Townships are restricted for large wind farms and large solar facilities only. The resolution states no megawatt figures.
